name: Colin Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play double bass in a theatre section, teach beginner bass on Saturdays and arrange simple parts when a school asks. I finished secondary school and still watch the senior player’s bow when an entrance is hard.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What brings you back, and what wears on you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the sound when the whole section finds the floor together. The theatre’s late call sheets wear me down, especially when the children need a pickup plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre strings that AI sorting a rehearsal list is harmless, but the orchestra still has to enter together. I would keep my double-bass chair and the Saturday pupils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have ten months of expenses saved and my partner’s library wage is steady. I am still junior in the orchestra, but a cancelled rehearsal does not put the mortgage at risk this month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will keep the Tuesday theatre rehearsals and Saturday beginner bass lessons this season. I would ask the stage manager for next quarter’s calls before accepting another private pupil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our bills. My part is hard enough without worrying about a new form on the manager’s desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when the theatre run ended early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The last theatre run ended early. My Saturday bass lessons covered my share of the mortgage after the theatre cancelled two shows. I would ask the union representative to check the cancellation clause before the next contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you still mark parts by hand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not use AI tools. I write the bowings in pencil because the young players can see the marks I changed after rehearsal.

I would keep the **cancellation clause** in the next contract.
think: Our **ten-month cushion** and library wage make one lost run manageable.
I am still **junior**, so I watch future theatre calls.
do: Keep **theatre rehearsals** and Saturday bass pupils this season.
Ask the **union representative** to check the next cancellation clause.
feel: I feel **calm** about household bills despite a shorter run.

fieldNote: His **strong cushion** and steady partner income protect the household from one short run.
He **avoids AI tools** and shows pupils his handwritten rehearsal changes.

steps.text: Keep Tuesday theatre rehearsals and Saturday beginner bass lessons

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that AI can write parts, schedule rehearsals and answer bookers, but fewer player hours need a proper discussion. I would ask the union for the hours in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My small arranging jobs may dry up, and the theatre may ask us to cover more shows with fewer rehearsals. Ten months saved protects the flat, not the quality of the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would compare my last two contracts with the next rehearsal schedule and take them to the union meeting. In the first year I would keep teaching beginners and ask two nearby theatres about openings only if my paid calls fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing my own arrangement fees and possibly hours. The cushion gives us time to decide, but it does not replace the pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take any other theatre opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not leave the theatre because of a rumour. I would apply only to an advertised paid post that accepts a player with my experience and fits school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the union to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union to show the actual hours, not merely say the software saves money. If rehearsals shrink, I want a written minimum before the next show.

say: I would ask for **paid rehearsal hours** in writing.
I would bring the **union** into any hour reduction.
think: My **arranging jobs** may disappear as software writes parts.
Fewer **rehearsals** could cut my pay and weaken the show.
do: Take two **theatre contracts** to the union meeting next month.
Ask about **advertised nearby posts** only if paid calls fall and experience and pickup fit.
feel: I feel **anxious** about possible loss of my own fees and hours.
S1.quote: Ten months saved protects the flat, not the quality of the work.
fieldNote: His own **arranging income** is exposed even with a strong reserve.
He wants **written minimums** and actual hours, with other posts only if suitable and advertised.

steps.text: Take two theatre contracts to union meeting about paid rehearsal hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that AGI by 2028 could make every score, but it must still pay the players who rehearse. I would ask the union to demand a written season schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my arranging fees to go in 2028 and some paid rehearsal hours may shrink. Robots that can play hands-on parts arrive around 2031, so the double-bass chair lasts longer, but the theatre can still cut a contract before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would bring my paid-hour records to the union and ask the theatre for next season’s written calls. If 2028 AGI reduces my paid hours, I would apply for an advertised paid bass post at a nearby theatre only if it accepts my experience and fits school pickup, and keep Saturday pupils until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the lost arrangements and the risk to rehearsals. Losing my arrangement fees in 2028 would hurt even with ten months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your cushion would you protect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep six months of household expenses untouched while looking. If one theatre needs a different qualification, I would not spend money applying there on hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner and children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner the arrangement fees are likely gone, not say the orchestra job is already lost. We would leave the children’s school routine alone until a real contract changes.

say: I would demand a **written season schedule** through the union.
I would say **live rehearsals** still deserve paid hours.
think: My **arrangement fees** likely end in 2028 before 2031 stage robots.
Theatre **rehearsal hours** may also be cut before robots arrive.
do: Take **paid-hour records** to the union this week.
Apply for an **advertised paid bass post** after 2028 hour cuts only if my experience qualifies and school pickup fits.
Keep **Saturday bass pupils** until a signed offer starts, protecting six months of savings during the search.
feel: I feel **anxious** about expected fees and possible hours lost.
S2.quote: Losing my arrangement fees in 2028 would hurt even with ten months saved.
fieldNote: He separates **2028 thinking-work loss** from the later 2031 robot effect on playing.
He protects a **six-month savings floor** while checking qualifications and waiting for signed offers.

steps.text: Bring paid-hour records to union before theatre season decision

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that AGI by 2031 gives us five years to bargain for paid rehearsal time and train newer string players. I would ask for a funded apprentice beside our section.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect arranging fees to end by 2031, but I could build more stable teaching before then. Robots around 2034 might play a bass onstage, though I do not know whether an audience would choose that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This autumn I would ask the theatre and union for a paid apprentice hour with a senior supervisor. If the theatre funds it, I would help the younger player on one rehearsal; in the first year after 2031 I would keep my paid teaching and check whether theatre calls remain in the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about arrangement income until teaching really replaces it. Five years is useful. A trainee place is not my own wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would the apprentice need a senior supervisor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A senior player must supervise because I am still learning the section myself. I would not take responsibility for a new player alone just to save the theatre a fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the theatre will not fund the place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the theatre refuses to fund it, I would keep asking the union to put the apprentice hour into the next contract. I would not ask the younger player to work free.

say: I would ask for a **funded apprentice hour** with supervision.
I would defend **paid rehearsals** during the five-year runway.
think: My **arranging fees** may end by 2031 before 2034 stage robots.
More **paid teaching** could replace fees if pupils keep booking.
do: Ask the **theatre and union** for a funded supervised apprentice hour this autumn.
Keep **paid bass lessons** after 2031 while pupils book, and check theatre calls against the contract.
feel: I feel **anxious** until teaching actually replaces lost arrangement pay.
S3.quote: A trainee place is not my own wage.
fieldNote: He insists on **senior supervision** because he remains a junior player himself.
His apprentice proposal requires **theatre funding**, and his own lost income still needs replacing.

steps.text: Ask union for funded apprentice hour with senior supervisor
Keep paid bass lessons after 2031 while pupils book

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children that AGI by 2036 leaves years to learn an instrument and to ask for fair work. I would keep playing at the theatre while the contract pays for a human section.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I might have enough teaching to live without arranging fees. Robots around 2039 could play the bass parts, but I cannot know whether the theatre would still want living players.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this year I would put half of each paid arrangement fee into savings until our reserve reaches twelve months. In the first year after 2036 I would compare paid theatre calls with last year and apply to an advertised local post only if calls fall and I qualify.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about the later stage question. Our current pay and ten months saved keep the next few years secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is twelve months already saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twelve months is a goal, not what is in the account today. If arranging work stops earlier, I would keep the ten-month cushion and save from teaching only when bills are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about unions and practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children to stand with other players and do their own work. A union can protect hours but cannot make me practise. They should learn to do both.

I would keep **paid theatre playing** while contracts support it.
think: More **paid teaching income** might replace arrangement work before 2036 if pupils keep booking.

do: Save half of each **paid arrangement fee** toward twelve months starting this year.
Apply for an **advertised local post** after 2036 only if theatre calls fall and I qualify.
Keep **paid theatre playing** while the contract supports a human bass section.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about later stages while current pay and savings hold.
S4.quote: A union can protect hours but cannot make me practise.
fieldNote: His twelve-month goal grows from **paid arrangements** and later paid teaching after bills.
He keeps a **ten-month reserve** if score work stops earlier and moves only for a qualifying vacancy.

steps.text: Save half of paid arrangement fees toward twelve months while fees continue

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because arrangement fees could go before the theatre decides its paid calls. A written schedule, a union review and a suitable advertised bass post would help me plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the young player while the senior one teaches. An unpaid chair does not become training just because the music sounds good.

headlineQuote: An unpaid chair does not become training just because the music sounds good.
portrait: At **43**, Colin is a junior theatre bassist with secondary school education, two children, a mortgage and ten months saved.
His partner’s **library wage** and nearby theatre posts strengthen his options despite exposed arrangement fees.
He avoids **AI tools** and seeks union records, paid rehearsal hours and funded senior supervision.
Across AGI dates he protects **teaching income** and savings, applying elsewhere only after real cuts and qualification checks.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end arrangement fees before the theatre confirms its paid calls.
whatWouldHelp: A **written season schedule**, union review and suitable advertised bass post would help Colin respond.
